intro: You're searching for a business will near you because you want your company shares, partnership interest or business property to pass on smoothly if you die. A business will is not the same as a personal will, and it needs to sit alongside your articles of association or partnership agreement. We can introduce you to a local wills and probate specialist who deals with business succession, and they will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a business will near me usually need
need_lead: A business will is about protecting the business you have built and the people who depend on it.
needs: You own shares in a private company and want them to pass to the right person without disrupting the business.
You are in a partnership and need your interest handled according to the partnership agreement.
You have business property, such as a farm or commercial premises, and want to consider business relief while rules are changing.
You want a separate business will that deals only with your business assets, leaving your personal will to cover family matters.
You need to check that your existing will and any shareholder agreement work together and do not conflict.
context_heading: What to understand about business wills and regulation
context: Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors (regulated by the SRA) and chartered legal executives (regulated by CILEx) are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly.

When choosing a provider, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and where your original will is stored. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction.

tell: The type of business you run, such as a limited company or partnership, and your role in it.

Whether there is a shareholder agreement or partnership agreement that deals with what happens on death.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate business will if I already have a personal will?
faqs.a: It depends on what your personal will says about your business assets. A separate business will can deal specifically with your shares, partnership interest or business property, and can be drafted to work alongside your existing will and any agreements. A specialist can look at your current arrangements and advise.

faqs.q: How does a business will interact with a shareholder agreement?
faqs.a: A shareholder agreement often sets out what happens to shares when a shareholder dies, such as whether the remaining shareholders have the option to buy them. A business will should be drafted to complement those terms, not contradict them. Your adviser will check both documents together.

faqs.q: What are the changes to business relief I keep hearing about?
faqs.a: Business relief rules are changing, and the details can affect how business property is treated for inheritance tax. Because the rules are evolving, it is important to get advice based on your own circumstances. A wills and probate specialist can explain the current position and how it might apply to you.

faqs.q: Is a business will legally binding in Scotland?
faqs.a: Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so a will made under English law may not be effective for Scottish business assets. If you have business interests in Scotland, you should make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction. iComply can introduce you to a specialist who works in the relevant area.

extra_heading: Why your search says "business will" rather than just "will"
extra: Typing "business will near me" suggests you already know that your business interests need separate thought from the rest of your estate. That instinct is usually right: shares in a private company, a partnership interest or business property such as a farm or commercial premises can pass in ways that surprise the people left behind if no will deals with them clearly. Wanting someone near you often means you would rather talk things through face to face than by email.

A common misunderstanding is that a business will replaces your personal will. In practice the two need to sit together, and both need to fit with your articles of association or partnership agreement, which may already say what happens to shares or partnership interests on death. Another misunderstanding is that business relief will look after everything automatically; the rules are changing, so it is worth asking how they apply to your particular assets rather than assuming.

When you compare local specialists, look at what they actually deal with rather than how close they are. Ask whether they handle business succession as well as personal wills, whether they are regulated and insured, and whether they will read your existing agreements before drafting anything. A first appointment usually covers your business structure, who you want to benefit, and what your agreements already require, so bring those documents with you if you can.

extra_faqs.q: Can one professional deal with both my personal will and my business will?
extra_faqs.a: Often yes, and there can be advantages in having one adviser see the whole picture so the two documents do not pull against each other. Ask at the outset whether they will look at your articles of association or partnership agreement as part of the work.

extra_faqs.q: What should I bring to a first meeting about a business will?
extra_faqs.a: Bring your existing will if you have one, your articles of association or partnership agreement, and a note of what shares, partnership interest or business property you hold. It also helps to say who you want to benefit and who else is involved in the business.

extra_faqs.q: Does it matter if my business is in Scotland?
extra_faqs.a: Yes. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so an adviser who practises in the right jurisdiction matters more than a short journey. Tell us where the business and its assets are based when you enquire.
